stem: A client with diabetes and loss of protective sensation in both feet says, “I only check my feet when they hurt.” Which response by the nurse is best?

options.A: Inspect both feet every day, including the soles and between the toes, because neuropathy can allow minor injuries to go unnoticed; use a mirror or ask for help if needed.
options.B: Check the feet only after walking long distances because painless injuries are unlikely during normal daily activity.
options.C: Rely on pain to identify early ulcers because diabetic neuropathy usually increases sensitivity to foot injury.
options.D: Inspect the feet once a month unless an open wound is already visible.

rationale: A is correct. The 2026 ADA Standards of Care recommend daily surveillance for early foot problems, particularly in people with loss of protective sensation, using visual inspection, palpation, or an unbreakable mirror when needed. Diabetic peripheral neuropathy can reduce or eliminate protective pain sensation, allowing minor trauma to go unrecognized and progress to ulceration or infection. B, C, and D delay detection and incorrectly rely on pain or infrequent inspection.
educational_objective: Teach clients with diabetic neuropathy or loss of protective sensation to inspect their feet every day so painless skin injuries or preulcerative changes can be identified and treated early.
source_organization: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee
source_document_title: Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
source_locator: Foot Care Recommendations 12.25 and 12.30; ‘Foot Care Education for People With Diabetes’ — people with sensory loss should have feet inspected at every visit and receive education on daily surveillance using palpation or visual inspection with an unbreakable mirror; LOPS predisposes to unrecognized minor trauma and diabetic foot ulceration
source_claim_supported: Loss of protective sensation can make foot trauma painless or unrecognized, and current ADA guidance recommends daily foot surveillance for early problems, with mirror or caregiver assistance when needed.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance — provide client education that promotes preventive self-care and reduces risk of chronic-disease complications
blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — preventive diabetic foot self-care
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source rationale-recall item into a client-teaching application question and reclassified it from infection control to Health Promotion and Maintenance. The final version uses current ADA 2026 daily-surveillance guidance and avoids implying that infection is the only reason for foot inspection.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.clinical_category: diabetic peripheral neuropathy / preventive foot care
audit_findings.source_audit: Verified directly against ADA Standards of Care 2026, Section 12. ADA recommends daily foot surveillance and explains that loss of protective sensation predisposes to unrecognized minor trauma and ulceration.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A reflects the daily-surveillance recommendation and sensory-loss mechanism without adding an unsupported examination interval beyond the source. The mirror/help language is explicitly supported.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; daily inspection is recommended because injury may be painless or unnoticed.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; injury can occur during ordinary activity and surveillance is daily, not activity-triggered.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; neuropathy can reduce pain/protective sensation.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; monthly inspection is inadequate for a client with loss of protective sensation.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A matches both the mechanism and current preventive-care recommendation.
audit_findings.cueing: All choices address inspection frequency and rationale; no unrelated distractor identifies the key.
audit_findings.blueprint: Health Promotion and Maintenance is appropriate because the central nursing task is preventive self-care education for a chronic disease complication.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked daily-versus-every-visit guidance, loss-of-protective-sensation mechanism, mirror/caregiver assistance, ulcer/infection progression wording, category mapping, and second-answer risk. No unresolved conflict remained.
